Tuning Connection Pools for a 10,000 RPS .NET Core API — .Net 10 Update

paragraphs.text: Calculating global database capacity based on per-pod concurrency limits is exactly how you prevent horizontal pod autoscaling from turning into an intentional distributed denial-of-service attack against your own database cluster. The breakdown of the exact math ($RPS \times \text{Query Time}$) and the introduction of partitioned DbContext pooling to mitigate lock contention are top-tier operational callouts for a 10,000 RPS scale.

However, when configuring AddDbContextPool with partitioned pools alongside ConfigureAwaitOptions.ForceYielding, how does the underlying architecture handle the risk of Thread Pool Starvation when an aggressive traffic spike saturates the partitionCount boundaries?

While ForceYielding mitigates synchronous blocking by forcing an immediate suspension and yield to the thread pool, doing this on high-frequency, ultra-short database executions (like a 20ms index lookup) can actually introduce a net-negative performance trade-off due to excessive context-switching overhead and repeated task scheduling cycles.

In a high-throughput, low-latency hot path, wouldn't a non-yielding async path that relies on fast asynchronous completion via ValueTask or standard Task completion states maximize throughput more predictably under heavy pool utilization?

paragraphs.text: A Note on Using AI for Learning: Throughout this guide, I’ll show you how to use ChatGPT (free) as a learning companion. Unlike GitHub Copilot, which integrates directly into your editor and could potentially send code snippets to Microsoft’s servers, using ChatGPT in your browser for learning is safer for understanding concepts. Never paste proprietary code into any AI tool — treat it like a tutor, not a pair programmer for commercial work. Use it to explain concepts, generate practice examples, and help you understand error messages. The prompts I provide are designed for learning, not for generating production code.

Great deep dive into ToonSharp!

paragraphs.text: Right now there isn’t a native browser parser like JSON.parse() for TOON, so a JS client would need a small parser library. Because JSON parsing in browsers is heavily optimized, it’ll almost always be faster than a custom JS parser.

So for SPAs (React/Angular), the 8% wire savings probably isn’t worth the extra parsing cost. TOON seems more suited to backend server-to-server communication, configs, or logs where readability and slightly smaller payloads matter more than client-side parsing speed.
